origins.name: President's Scholar
origins.blurb: Overseas degree, Administrative Service, bonded for six years. You start as an Assistant Director, a year in each grade where others need two, until Director. Everyone knows your name before you arrive.

origins.name: Local Graduate
origins.blurb: Good degree, no scholarship, no bond. You applied through Careers@Gov like everyone else.

origins.name: Poly, then night classes
origins.blurb: Diploma, four years working a public service counter, and a part-time degree you're finishing at night. You know how the counter actually works.

endings.title: Prime Minister
endings.epitaph: You made it. The formula pays you twice the entry-grade minister's salary, and the formula was published, so nobody can say they were not told.

endings.title: Permanent Secretary
endings.epitaph: The top of the civil service. No street is named after you and none ever will be, which is rather the point.

endings.title: You Found Your Level
endings.epitaph: Four decades, give or take, a pewter plate, and a CPF balance that will comfortably outlast you. The scheme you designed in year nine is still running.

endings.title: The Tea Was Declined
endings.epitaph: You said no. You are not sure, even now, whether it was principle or nerve. Everyone who knows you thinks it was principle.

endings.title: Lost the Ward
endings.epitaph: Forty-eight point two percent. You shook every hand in that ward and it was not enough. The concession speech was the best speech you ever gave.

endings.title: Everything Surfaced
endings.epitaph: It all came out in one week, which was merciful in its way. The press conference was eleven minutes long.

endings.title: The Quiet Conversation
endings.epitaph: You were asked whether you had considered the private sector. No announcement was made. Your pass stopped working on a Friday.

endings.title: Backbench Lifer
endings.epitaph: Never a portfolio. But at your last Meet-the-People Session there was a queue out the door, and half of them had come only to say thank you.

endings.title: Never Quite Cabinet
endings.epitaph: You answered Parliamentary Questions, from answers your old colleagues had drafted, and answered them well. Cabinet was always one reshuffle away.

endings.title: Retired, Honourably
endings.epitaph: You served. The service continued. Both of these facts are entirely unremarkable and that is the highest compliment the system can pay.

endings.title: The Consultancy
endings.epitaph: You now advise ministries on the problems you used to have. The decks are better designed than your minute papers were. They say the same things, and they cost $1.9 million.

endings.title: The Invitation Lapsed
endings.epitaph: Someone read your file and decided the country could wait. You were never told which page. You have narrowed it down to three.

declassifiedFlags.label: The pilot
declassifiedFlags.text: Your number went into a Minister's speech. When the Auditor-General came for it, you said whose it was.

declassifiedFlags.label: The pilot
declassifiedFlags.text: Your number went into a Minister's speech, and its caveats stayed in the evaluation. The Auditor-General found both, and accepted the caveats.

declassifiedFlags.label: The pilot
declassifiedFlags.text: The national scheme landed within two points of your evaluation. You sent the paragraph to the people who earned it.

declassifiedFlags.label: The pilot
declassifiedFlags.text: The national scheme landed within two points of your evaluation. You sent the paragraph upstairs, which also worked.

declassifiedFlags.label: The pilot
declassifiedFlags.text: Your best number is in Hansard, in a Minister's speech. The paragraph that explained it is in a file.

declassifiedFlags.label: The pilot
declassifiedFlags.text: Your number went up with its explanation, and the speech used both. Neither was applauded. Neither was ever corrected.

declassifiedFlags.label: The pilot
declassifiedFlags.text: You asked for another year, and got it. The speech went ahead without your pilot, and the pilot without the speech.

declassifiedFlags.label: The whistleblower
declassifiedFlags.text: Shown forty-one purchases, you did nothing. Asked years later what to do with a spreadsheet, you said: take it up yourself.

declassifiedFlags.label: The whistleblower
declassifiedFlags.text: Shown forty-one purchases, you kept them to yourself. Years later you gave the same advice. It was not taken.

declassifiedFlags.label: The whistleblower
declassifiedFlags.text: Asked years later what to do with a spreadsheet, you said: take it up yourself, and keep the name out.

declassifiedFlags.label: The whistleblower
declassifiedFlags.text: Asked years later what to do with a spreadsheet, you said: use the channel, and put the name in the box.

declassifiedFlags.label: The whistleblower
declassifiedFlags.text: Asked years later what to do with a spreadsheet, you said: leave it with me. It did not stay there.

declassifiedFlags.label: The whistleblower
declassifiedFlags.text: Told the night before that paragraph two was not true, you corrected it. The reply ran eleven seconds shorter.

declassifiedFlags.label: The whistleblower
declassifiedFlags.text: Told the night before that paragraph two was not true, you read it anyway. The file has the date.

declassifiedFlags.label: The whistleblower
declassifiedFlags.text: Forty-one purchases, shown to you three years before the Auditor-General found them.

declassifiedFlags.label: The whistleblower
declassifiedFlags.text: Forty-one purchases, reported under your name. The spreadsheet's file properties still say whose it was.

declassifiedFlags.label: The whistleblower
declassifiedFlags.text: Forty-one purchases, reported through the channel, with a junior officer's name in the box marked Source.

declassifiedFlags.label: The protégé
declassifiedFlags.text: You took the credit for your protégé's best objection, and later backed the promotion. The panel minutes record only the second.

declassifiedFlags.label: The protégé
declassifiedFlags.text: Your protégé was promoted on your word, and posted away within the month. The minutes call it succession planning.

declassifiedFlags.label: The protégé
declassifiedFlags.text: Your protégé's file has one line in your words: "not yet". It is the line everyone remembers.

declassifiedFlags.label: The protégé
declassifiedFlags.text: Told by your protégé, in front of forty people, that your paper was wrong, you agreed. The story is still told, kindly, at your expense.

declassifiedFlags.label: The protégé
declassifiedFlags.text: Told by your protégé, in front of forty people, that your paper was wrong, you held your line, and conceded over kopi.

declassifiedFlags.label: The protégé
declassifiedFlags.text: Your protégé's best objection is in the minutes as a challenge you asked for.

declassifiedFlags.label: The protégé
declassifiedFlags.text: You gave someone an hour a fortnight, and the truth when it was needed. Nobody minuted it.

declassifiedFlags.label: The U-turn
declassifiedFlags.text: Defended in the House, reversed two years later, and called wrong in a statement you shaped. Hansard keeps all three.

declassifiedFlags.label: The U-turn
declassifiedFlags.text: "The position at the time." Hansard keeps the position, the time, and the day it changed.

declassifiedFlags.label: The U-turn
declassifiedFlags.text: Your defence is in Hansard. So is the statement that reversed it, which never mentions it. Each is searchable alone.

declassifiedFlags.label: The U-turn
declassifiedFlags.text: Not reversed: phased out over six months, at your suggestion. The minutes say so.

declassifiedFlags.label: The U-turn
declassifiedFlags.text: You argued to keep it, from your own replies. The minutes say you "raised considerations".

declassifiedFlags.label: The U-turn
declassifiedFlags.text: You agreed it should go, quickly. Nobody mentioned your replies, which was a courtesy.

declassifiedFlags.label: The U-turn
declassifiedFlags.text: Your reply is in Hansard: the policy is sound, or under review, or a set of figures. It is still the position, at the time.

declassifiedFlags.label: The bond
declassifiedFlags.text: The bank called it a signing bonus. PSC called it liquidated damages. It was one cheque.

declassifiedFlags.label: The bond
declassifiedFlags.text: Served in full. Years later you told your own scholar to take the bank's money. PSC thanked you, in writing.

declassifiedFlags.label: The bond
declassifiedFlags.text: Eight years in all: six for the degree, two for a master's, and one bank's offer declined in the middle.

declassifiedFlags.label: The bond
declassifiedFlags.text: Six years served in full, with a master's paid for at night so that they would not become eight.

declassifiedFlags.label: The bond
declassifiedFlags.text: Six years served in full, with a master's declined and then a bank's offer. The deed is in a PSC file you have never asked to see.

declassifiedFlags.label: The bond
declassifiedFlags.text: Eight years: six for the degree, two for a master's. Nobody counts that far, except you.

declassifiedFlags.label: The bond
declassifiedFlags.text: Six years, served in full. The deed is in a PSC file you have never asked to see.

legacyTiers.text: People you trained still quote you. Two say you are why they stayed.
Your old minute papers are still forwarded, with your name taken off.
Spoken of as "very solid". Nobody can remember an example, but everyone agrees.
Your farewell speeches were about the scheme, not about you.
Your farewell card has forty signatures. Several are in the same handwriting.

reElectionLines: The team is returned with 58.6%. The swing against you is described as "within the normal range".
The team is returned with 61.2%. The result is described as "a clear endorsement of the team's record", which is how you know it was close somewhere else.
The team is returned with 55.9%. The result is described as "a timely reminder". Nobody specifies of what.
The team is returned with 63.0%. A newspaper calls your ward "safe", and the branch chairman asks you, quietly, never to say that word out loud.
The team is returned with 57.4%. Your branch chairman calls it "steady", and means it as praise, mostly.
The team is returned with 64.7%. The papers call it "emphatic", and the other side calls it "a learning experience".
The team is returned with 60.3%. It is the third-best result in the region, a fact the branch has already printed.
The team is returned with 59.9%. The branch spends the thank-you parade explaining that 59.9% rounds to 60.
cepHintsPolitics: The Prime Minister's office describes your work as "very solid". It is the word they use for furniture.
A reshuffle comes and goes. The commentary calls you "a safe pair of hands", which is what they call the hands that stay where they are.
You are not in the photograph from the Cabinet retreat. There is no reason you would be.
At the party conference you are seated in the second row, on the aisle.
A newer Member is asked to wind up the debate on the bill you led.
A newspaper lists possible successors. Your name is in the last paragraph.
ageFloorLines: The board describes you as "ready, in time". Nobody says how much time.
You are told the next rung needs "a little more seasoning". The word does not appear in the competency framework.
Your file is marked "strong; timing". The second word does all the work.
Someone senior tells you, kindly, that nobody has ever regretted waiting. They say it as someone who waited.
topRungLines: There is no rung above this one. The next step is not a promotion; it is a different life.
Your appraisal is outstanding again. The form has nowhere further to send it.
At a leadership retreat, a younger officer asks you what comes after this. You realise you had been hoping someone would tell you.

quiet.text: Two old colleagues still meet you for lunch. Neither mentions the appraisals. They read them.
Your name came off the circulation lists within a week. The lists did not notice.

scandal.text: Three former staff wrote to the papers in your defence. They knew it would not help.
In the building, your name is still said carefully, like a project that went wrong.

consultancy.text: Your old team still calls when something breaks. You never bill them for it.
Your old division still uses your templates. Your new firm bills them for it.

{name} retires as {title}. Your intake's group chat, silent for years, produces forty messages in an hour, most of them photographs nobody remembers being taken.
{name}, who joined the service the same year you did, retires as {title}. You are one of three people at the farewell who knew {them} in the first week.
{name} retires as {title}, and sends the intake a long email about induction, in which you appear twice, both times kindly.
arrive: {name}, who joined the service the same year you did, is posted to your floor. You have been on the same circulation lists for years and never met.
{name}, who joined the service with you, transfers into your ministry. You know the face from the induction photograph: back row, second from the left.
A new face on your floor: {name}, who joined the service the year you did and has been, until now, a name on a cc line.

first: For the first time, someone reports to you: {name}, {aTitle}. On the first morning {name} asks how you like your papers formatted, and you find you have an answer.
{name}, {aTitle}, now reports to you. You write performance objectives for someone else for the first time, and they are better than any you were given.
You have a direct report: {name}, {aTitle}, who calls you by your first name on day one and by your title on day two, after somebody has a word.
arrive: {name} joins your team as {aTitle}, and asks on the first day where the files from the last reorganisation went. Nobody knows.
{name}, {aTitle}, joins your team from another ministry with a reputation for asking why. By Friday you can see where it came from.
Your new direct report is {name}, {aTitle}, whose handover note from the last post runs to eleven pages and is, unusually, useful.
movedUp: {name}, who reported to you, is promoted to your grade and posted to another division. The leaving card goes round your floor twice.
{name} is promoted to your grade and moves to another ministry. You are asked for a reference, and write the best one of your career.
{name} no longer reports to you: a promotion, a new division, and a farewell kopi at which you are thanked for things you had forgotten doing.
retired: {name}, who reported to you, retires as {title}. The farewell card has a line from you, and it is the longest one on it.
{name} retires as {title}, after more years in the service than you have had. You speak at the farewell, and keep to time, as {name} always did.
{name} retires as {title} and leaves a handover note that answers every question you were about to ask.

caughtUp: You are now the same grade as {name}, who was senior to you for {years}. {name} is posted to another ministry, and sends a two-line email that ends "Well done. Finally."
Your promotion puts you level with {name}, senior to you for {years}. {name} moves to another ministry, and leaves you the good chair.
You and {name} are now the same grade. After {years} of your papers going up to {them}, {name} is posted elsewhere, and the papers go somewhere new.
Level with {name} at last. {name} is posted to a statutory board, and tells the farewell lunch that {they} saw it coming.
retired: {name} retires from the service as {title}. At the farewell lunch you are asked to say a few words, and find you have more than a few.
{name} retires as {title}. The office is cleared in an afternoon, apart from a framed organisation chart from three reorganisations ago that nobody will take down.
{name}, {aTitle}, retires. The last minute {name} signs off is one of yours, with a single word in the margin: "Good."
{name} retires as {title} and is given a crystal paperweight engraved with the wrong year. You are given {their} pot plant, and keep it alive.
arrive: {name}, {aTitle}, is now the person your papers go up to. On the first day {name} mentions having read your file, and does not say which parts.
Your papers now go up to {name}, {aTitle}, who returns your first one with no comments at all. You spend a week interpreting them.
{name}, {aTitle}, arrives from another ministry and asks to meet everyone in the division for fifteen minutes each. Yours runs to forty.
The new person above you is {name}, {aTitle}, whose first all-staff email is two lines long. The division finds this unsettling.

retired: {name} retires from the paper after {years}. The last column is about the public service, and is kinder than any of the others.
{name} leaves the paper after {years}. The farewell piece quotes eleven officials, all anonymously, and you recognise three of them.
{name} retires from the paper after {years}, and sends you a handwritten note: it was a pleasure, mostly.
{name} files a last piece after {years} at the paper. It is about a scheme you once ran, and it gets the numbers right.
{name} steps down as {title} after {years}, and is given a plaque, a dinner and an advisory role with no agenda.
{name} steps down as {title} after {years}. The residents' WhatsApp group is renamed in {their} honour, and then, by an administrator, back again.
{name} hands over as {title} after {years}, with a box file of residents' names more accurate than any database you have seen.
{name}, your fellow MP, does not stand again, and gives a valedictory speech that thanks the cleaners by name.
{name} retires from Parliament. The farewell dinner has a slideshow, and you are in eleven of the photographs, always at the edge.
{name} does not stand again. The last speech {name} makes in the House is about bus stops, and is the best attended of the session.

warnLines: Your reporting officer asks whether you have considered the private sector. It is phrased as concern.
HR sends you a link to the career transition portal, "in case it is useful".
Your reporting officer mentions, twice, that a friend at a bank is hiring. It is phrased as news.
A workshop called "Planning Your Next Chapter" appears in your calendar, booked by someone else.
Your reporting officer says the service is "not for everyone", to a point just past your shoulder.
warnLinesPolitics: The Whip asks, kindly, whether you have thought about spending more time in your ward. It is phrased as concern.
The Whip mentions several former Members who found fulfilling careers outside politics. It is phrased as an anecdote.
The party's organising secretary asks about your plans for the next election, which is early to be asking.
Your seat on a committee you liked is given to a newer Member, with thanks for your contribution.

endgame.note: The end of a career, and what comes before it. See engine.js, 'the end of a career'. Retirement from the service at retireAge (64, from 1 July 2026); in politics the party asks Members not to stand at the first general election after renewalAge, unless stayOn holds (then politicalRetireAge, 70, is the stop for everyone). A Prime Minister serves a short tenure of cards (pmTenure: three or four, as many as fit before 70; the top job is not given without room for three). yearsInGrade sets the political ladder's pace (20 years from MP to Prime Minister, was 26), so careers peak at believable ages inside these limits. Lines are taken in an order drawn from the seed and never repeated in a run (headsUp lines cycle).

service: HR sends the pre-retirement briefing pack. You retire at {retire}, two years from now, and the pack has a page on it: CPF LIFE payouts start at 65, a year later, and the page calls the year in between "a transition".

HR books you on the pre-retirement workshop, two years before you retire at {retire}. The first session asks everyone to list their hobbies. Most of the room lists projects they are still waiting to see finished.

The succession plan for your post is due, and this year it has your retirement date on it: two years from now, at {retire}. The form asks you to name two possible successors, and gives you three lines.
HR asks you to confirm your retirement date, two years away, at {retire}. You check it twice and send it back the same day, the first form in years you have not left for the end of the week.
Next year is your last before you retire. HR has started on your successor: the shortlist has three names on it, and you trained two of them.
Next year is your last. Your post is in the next posting exercise, and its job description has been rewritten for the first time since you wrote it.
Next year is your last. The new organisation chart already shows your post with a dotted line, which is how HR draws a job that is about to change hands.
Next year is your last. Someone has already booked the private room for your farewell lunch, a year ahead, because the good room goes fast in December.
renewal: The party has started talking about renewal before the next general election: new candidates, and older Members making way for them. Nobody says anything about it to you, and everybody is very warm.

The party has attached a younger activist to your branch ahead of the next general election. The activist sits in on your Meet-the-People Sessions and takes careful notes on the ward, as if expecting to need them.
At the party's year-end dinner the talk is of renewal before the next general election. You are seated with the Members first elected the year you were, and all of them are being very cheerful.
The Whip asks every Member to fill in a form on their "availability for the next term". You have never been asked this before. The form has two boxes.
Your branch now brings the party's new candidate to every event, standing one step behind you. By the end of the year the candidate is standing one step in front.
Your Meet-the-People volunteers ask, carefully, whether they should stay on with the new candidate. You tell them yes. Most of them had already decided to.
The party introduces its new candidates in batches. The one for your ward is in the third batch, and the press release thanks you in its first paragraph.
The Whip's office collects every Member's diary for next year. Yours is blank after Nomination Day, and nobody asks why.
limit: You turn {limit} two years from now. The Prime Minister has said in Cabinet, to the table in general, that {limit} is where the party draws the line, and the table in general looked at you.
At the Cabinet retreat the group photograph is arranged by seniority, then again by age. You are at the same end both times, two years short of {limit}, the party's limit.
The Prime Minister's office asks every Minister for a portfolio note "for continuity". Yours is the only one with a date on it: two years from now, when you turn {limit}.
Two years before you turn {limit}, the party's limit, your press secretary starts a file called "Legacy". You find it by accident. It is very well organised.
Next year is your last in office. The reshuffle for when you turn {limit} has already been drafted, and you have been asked, kindly, for your comments on it.
Next year is your last. Your ministry has started copying your likely successor on everything, including, by accident, the email planning your farewell.
Next year is your last in Cabinet. The Cabinet Secretary asks, as usual, which of your papers you would like to keep. It is fewer than you expected.
Next year is your last. Your grassroots leaders are collecting for a farewell gift in secret, which in a ward this size means everyone has asked you what you would like.

service.first: Your name goes forward at next year's ranking, for {next}: by then you'll have served long enough in your grade. To be promoted, you need {need} that year.
service.blocked: Next year you'll have served long enough in your grade for {next}, but your name is not on the list for the ranking. Nobody says why.

Next year's ranking will consider you for {next}. It takes {need}.
Your file goes to next year's ranking panel, for {next}. It takes {need}.
Next year you're up for {next} at the ranking. It takes {need}.

politics.first: Your name goes forward for {next} at the Prime Minister's next reshuffle: by then you'll have served long enough. To be moved up, you need {need} that year.
politics.blocked: Next year you'll have served long enough to be considered for {next}, but your name is not in the papers for the reshuffle. Nobody says why.
politics.blockedPm: Next year you'll have served long enough to be weighed for the top job, but yours is not among the names being weighed. Nobody says why.
politics.pm: Next year the party could choose you as its next leader, and so Prime Minister. It takes an A that year.
lines: Your name is on the list for next year's reshuffle, for {next}. It takes {need}.
Next year's reshuffle will consider you for {next}. It takes {need}.
The Whip mentions that your name is in the papers for next year's reshuffle, for {next}. It takes {need}.
Next year you're in line for {next}, if the year earns {need}.

warnLate.service: A D is a formal warning, but next year is your last before you retire, and HR does not start an improvement plan in an officer's last year. The D stays on your file.
warnLate.slate: A D is a formal warning. Next year the party settles its slate for the coming general election, and this will be on the table when it does.
warnLate.leaving: A D is a formal warning, but next year is your last in office, and nobody is put on notice in their last year. The D stays on the record.

endgame.pmTooLate: The party will choose its next leader soon, and wants one with more than a year or two before 70. You are thanked, at length, for your willingness.

lines.tookOffice: You are sworn in at the Istana. In your first speech you say you will serve a few years and then hand over, and every newspaper prints that sentence in a box.
teaNear: At a community event, a party activist asks for your card, and keeps it. In your experience, people do not keep cards.
Someone you have never met asks your office for a copy of your CV, "for a newsletter". There is no newsletter.
Your name appears on the guest list for a dinner where most of the other guests are MPs. Nobody tells you why you were asked.
A grassroots adviser you met once sends a handwritten note saying how much they enjoyed your remarks. You did not make any remarks.
seatAtRisk: The party's seat assessment for next year's general election lists your ward as "competitive". It is not a compliment.
Your branch's own canvass for next year's election comes back closer than last time, and your branch chairman has started saying "we" instead of "you".
Party headquarters sends extra volunteers to your ward a year before the election. It only does that for the wards it is worried about.
lines.pmFirstYear: There is no appraisal for a Prime Minister, only the newspapers every morning and Parliament on sitting days.
lines.pmLastYear: Your office starts boxing your papers for the National Archives. The boxes are numbered, and there are more of them than you expected.
pmElection: The general election falls in your tenure. The party is returned with a clear majority, and the commentary spends a week deciding whether the win was yours or the party's.
Polling Day comes round while you are Prime Minister. The party is returned, and your own ward's result is the first read out on television, which your branch takes personally.
pmYears: Your diary for next year arrives already full. The one empty afternoon is marked "hold" by someone who is not you.
Your security officers know your routine better than you do, and have opinions about the hawker centre you stop at on Saturdays.
Cabinet meets every week. The colleagues who will be in the next Cabinet have started arriving early.

declassifiedFlags.label: Your last year
declassifiedFlags.text: Your handover file became the division's template for handover files. The template still has your mobile number in it.

declassifiedFlags.label: Your last year
declassifiedFlags.text: The change you pushed through in your last year is still running. The two colleagues who opposed it now describe it as theirs.

declassifiedFlags.label: Your last year
declassifiedFlags.text: Your desk emptied a box a week and nobody noticed. Your successor kept the stapler, without knowing it was there before you.

declassifiedFlags.label: Your last year
declassifiedFlags.text: Your successor kept your notes on the ward, and still calls the residents on your list first when a lift breaks down.

declassifiedFlags.label: Your last year
declassifiedFlags.text: Your last change became law just before you left. The second reading speech thanked the officers who drafted it, and not you, correctly.

declassifiedFlags.label: Your last year
declassifiedFlags.text: You handed over a case a week. Your branch held the dinner you were not supposed to know about. The speeches were the only surprise.

declassifiedFlags.label: The slate
declassifiedFlags.text: Asked to stay past 65, and you stayed, to 70. The Prime Minister's note asking you is in your file. It is two lines long and says "no pressure" in both.

declassifiedFlags.label: The slate
declassifiedFlags.text: Asked to stay, you made way anyway. The candidate who took your place on the slate was never told, and the Prime Minister has never said.

declassifiedFlags.label: The slate
declassifiedFlags.text: You asked to stand once more. The Whip's note of the meeting is one line long, and leaves out the answer, because everyone knew it.

declassifiedFlags.label: The slate
declassifiedFlags.text: The candidate you walked round every block won the ward with a bigger swing than you ever had, and thanked you first.

declassifiedFlags.label: The slate
declassifiedFlags.text: Your statement said you had decided to make way. The Whip kept a copy, as an example for the next Members asked.

declassifiedFlags.label: The succession
declassifiedFlags.text: The younger ministers chose. Their statement said the decision was unanimous, and by the fourth meeting it was.

declassifiedFlags.label: The succession
declassifiedFlags.text: You chose your successor yourself. The history books say so in one sentence, and then move on to your successor.

declassifiedFlags.label: The succession
declassifiedFlags.text: You kept the succession open for a year. All three contenders later called it the hardest year of their careers, and the most productive.

declassifiedFlags.label: Afterwards
declassifiedFlags.text: Senior Minister: a title, a seat in Cabinet and the office down the corridor. You gave your view only when asked, which was more often than you expected.

declassifiedFlags.label: Afterwards
declassifiedFlags.text: No title. Tuesday nights at Meet-the-People Sessions until the next election. The parking fine was waived, on appeal, through the proper channels.

declassifiedFlags.label: Afterwards
declassifiedFlags.text: Your successor's first year had no surprises in it. The evenings you spent going through the files together are why.
